reading.p: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church believes in the intercession (prayer) of the Holy Virgin Mary, the Angels, and all the Saints. A common objection is raised against this belief: "But doesn't the Bible say there is only one mediator?"

reading.quote: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.
We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

reading.p: Our answer is yes, and we agree completely. The confusion comes from not understanding the different types of mediation that exist.
Christ's advocacy is propitiatory. This means He paid the price for our sin. His advocacy is based on His sacrifice and His blood, and He is the only one who can do this, for He is our Redeemer.

The saints' intercession, by contrast, is supplicatory. This simply means praying for someone. Their intercession is merely a prayer offered on our behalf to Christ. They are not redeeming us; they are praying for us.
Scripture makes this clear. Christ is our Advocate precisely because He is our propitiation, the payment for our sins.

reading.quote: If any man sin, we have an advocate... Jesus Christ the righteous: And He is the propitiation for our sins...
...one mediator... Christ Jesus; Who gave Himself a ransom for all.

reading.p: No saint, angel, or human being can pay for your sins. Only Jesus Christ can. This is His unique and un-shareable role.

reading.h2: God Loves and Asks for Intercession

reading.p: The Old Testament is filled with examples of God requiring the intercession of His righteous ones as a condition for forgiveness. This is not to say that God cannot forgive directly; He can. Rather, He does it to honor His saints and to teach us about the power of prayer and unity. Intercession is a clear example of how Orthodox Christians derive their practices from the Bible.
God commands intercession. In Genesis 20:1-7, King Abimelech takes Sarah, not knowing she is Abraham's wife, and God warns him in a dream.

reading.quote: Now therefore restore the man his wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live.

reading.p: The lesson is striking: God Himself made Abraham's prayer a condition for Abimelech's life.

reading.h2: Biblical Proof (Part 2): Job and His Friends

reading.p: God requires intercession. In Job 42:7-8, God is angry with Job's three friends for their foolish words.

reading.quote: Therefore... go to my servant Job... and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept; lest I deal with you after your folly.

reading.p: God's forgiveness was tied directly to the intercession of His servant Job.

Here we see intercession "for the sake of" others. In Genesis 18:17-32, God tells Abraham that He is about to destroy Sodom, giving him the chance to intercede. Abraham bargains with God, asking, "Wilt thou also destroy the righteous with the wicked?"

reading.quote: If I find in Sodom fifty righteous... then I will spare all the place for their sakes.

reading.p: God agrees, and He would have saved the whole city for the sake of just ten righteous people.

Intercession changes the outcome. In Exodus 32:7-14, the people make the golden calf, and God tells Moses He will destroy them. Moses pleads with God, "Turn from Thy fierce wrath... Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Thy servants..."

reading.quote: And the Lord repented of the evil which He thought to do unto His people.

reading.p: Moses' intercession saved the people.

reading.h2: What About Those Already in Heaven?

reading.p: Does this power stop at death? No. God continues to honor His saints long after they have departed. In 1 Kings 11:12-13, God is angry with Solomon and says He will tear the kingdom away from him.

reading.quote: ...notwithstanding in thy days I will not do it for David thy father's sake... I will give one tribe to thy son for David my servant's sake...

reading.p: King David had long departed, but God still showed mercy for his sake.

reading.quote: I beseech you... that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me...

reading.p: If St. Paul, a living saint, asked for the prayers of other living people, and if we ask our friends and family—who are still striving and sinning—to pray for us, then why would we not ask for the prayers of those who have finished their course, who are perfected in heaven, and who are living in Paradise with Christ? Have they become less able to pray now that they are in God's presence, or are they more able?

reading.h3: How can the saints in heaven even hear us?

reading.p: Their knowledge is perfected. They know more in heaven, not less, and they are no longer limited by a physical body.

reading.quote: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.

reading.h3: Proof That They Know What Is Happening on Earth

reading.quote: Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.

reading.p: How could they rejoice if they did not know it had happened?

reading.quote: The twenty-four elders in heaven have golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of the saints.

reading.p: How could they offer our prayers if they did not receive them? Likewise, in Luke 16:25-29, Abraham in Paradise knows all about the lives of both Lazarus and the rich man, and he even knows about "Moses and the prophets," who came hundreds of years after him.

The Angels are also powerful intercessors. In Zechariah 1:12 the angel of the Lord prays, "O Lord of hosts, how long wilt Thou not have mercy on Jerusalem," and God accepted his prayer. Hebrews 1:14 calls the angels "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation," showing that they are actively working for us. And in Genesis 48:16, Jacob blesses Joseph's sons, saying, "The Angel which redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads" — an "Angel" the Fathers understand to be the pre-incarnate Word of God, since redemption belongs to God alone.

The goal is Theosis (deification)—becoming by grace what God is by nature. For us as Orthodox, the goal of salvation is not merely "getting into heaven" or "being forgiven." The goal is to become "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4); God's plan is to make us like Him by grace.

How does intercession accomplish this? God is Love. He is a Trinity, a perfect communion of love between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. To become like God, we ourselves must become beings of perfect love. Sin is selfishness and isolation; love is the opposite, for it is relational and self-giving.

When God invites us to pray for one another, He is training us in love. He is calling us out of our selfish isolation to participate in the care of others. When we intercede, we are acting like God, who cares for all.

reading.h2: Summary: Why We Ask for Intercession

list: We do not "pray to" the saints. We ask for their prayers (their intercession), just as we ask our friends on earth.
To honor them. God Himself honors them by accepting their prayers: "If any man serve me, him will my Father honour" (John 12:26).
Because they are alive. We believe in the life of the world to come.
For humility. We show humility by admitting that we need the prayers of those who are holier than we are.
For unity. We believe in One Church, the Body of Christ, which is not broken by death; we are all connected, the perfect communion of saints.

studyGuide.overview: This lesson explains the Ethiopian Orthodox practice of asking for the intercession of the Holy Virgin Mary, the angels, and the saints, while fully affirming that Christ is the one Mediator. It distinguishes Christ's unique propitiatory mediation, based on His sacrifice, from the supplicatory intercession of the saints, which is simply prayer offered on our behalf, and it grounds this teaching in many biblical examples.
keyPoints: Christ is the one and only propitiatory Mediator; His advocacy rests on His sacrifice and blood, and no one else can pay for sin.
The saints' intercession is supplicatory, meaning prayer on our behalf to Christ, not redemption.
God Himself often required the intercession of the righteous, as with Abraham, Job, and Moses.
God honors His saints even after death, showing mercy to Solomon for David's sake.
If we ask living people to pray for us, it is reasonable to ask the perfected saints in heaven, who are more able to pray.
Scripture shows the saints and angels know what happens on earth and offer the prayers of the faithful.
The ultimate goal of intercession is Theosis: being trained in self-giving love within the one communion of saints.
reviewQuestions: What is the difference between propitiatory and supplicatory mediation?
How does asking the saints to pray for us not contradict 1 Timothy 2:5?
What do the examples of Abraham, Job, and Moses teach about God asking for intercession?
How does the lesson show that God honors His saints even after they have died?
What scriptural reasons are given that the saints in heaven can hear and offer our prayers?
How does the practice of intercession serve the goal of Theosis?

checks: Christ confessed as the one, unique, un-shareable propitiatory Mediator (1 Tim 2:5; 1 John 2:1-2), fully sound.
Saints' role limited to supplicatory prayer to Christ; explicitly states 'we do not pray to them' but ask their prayers.
Veneration/honor of saints and angels clearly distinguished from the worship and redemption due to Christ alone.
Intercession of the Theotokos, angels, and saints affirmed in line with Ethiopian Tewahedo teaching.
Trinity described as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in perfect communion of love; no Filioque asserted.
Theosis presented as becoming by grace what God is by nature (2 Peter 1:4), consistent with Orthodox doctrine.
